title: Proportional Reasoning-1
subject: Maths-1
description: Ratios, proportions, the Rule of Three, sharing in a ratio, changing mixtures and unit conversions from NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 Chapter 7.

questions.question: In the chapter's set of five tiger images of different sizes, which images looked similar to one another?
questions.explanation: A (60 × 40), C (30 × 20) and D (90 × 60) all have width : height = 3 : 2, so they look alike. B is elongated and E is compressed.

questions.question: Image A is 60 mm × 40 mm and image C is 30 mm × 20 mm. By what factor did BOTH the width and the height change from A to C?
questions.explanation: 30 ÷ 60 = ½ and 20 ÷ 40 = ½. Because width and height changed by the same factor, A and C look similar.

questions.question: Image B (40 mm × 20 mm) was obtained from A (60 mm × 40 mm) by taking 20 mm off both the width and the height. Why does B look distorted?
options: Its height is 2/3 of A's but its width is only 1/2 of A's — different factors
A rectangle can never look similar to another rectangle of a smaller size
Its width is 2/3 of A's but its height is only 1/2 of A's — different factors
Both sides lost exactly 20 mm, so the factors of change are also equal
questions.explanation: 40/60 = 2/3 but 20/40 = 1/2. Subtracting the same amount does not multiply both sides by the same factor, so the shape stretches (B looks elongated).

questions.question: By what factor do the width and height of image D (90 mm × 60 mm) change compared with image A (60 mm × 40 mm)?
questions.explanation: 90 ÷ 60 = 3/2 and 60 ÷ 40 = 3/2. Same factor for both, so D is similar to A (D is the enlarged version).

questions.question: A 60 mm × 40 mm photo is resized so that it still looks similar. Which new size is correct?
questions.explanation: 45/60 = 3/4 and 30/40 = 3/4 — same factor. In 50 × 30 the factors are 5/6 and 3/4; in 45 × 25 they are 3/4 and 5/8; 80 × 60 is 4 : 3, not 3 : 2.

questions.question: Which statement about the five tiger images is NOT correct?
options: Image D is the largest of the three similar-looking images
Image B looks compressed and fatter than the other images
Images A, C and D all have the width-to-height ratio 3 : 2
Image E has a width-to-height ratio of 1 : 1 in simplest form
questions.explanation: The chapter says the tiger appears ELONGATED in B and compressed and fatter in E (the square). The other three statements match the measurement table.

questions.question: Image E (60 mm × 60 mm) looks different from image A because E is a square while A has a width-to-height ratio of 3 : 2.
questions.explanation: 60 : 60 reduces to 1 : 1, so E is a square; A is 60 : 40 = 3 : 2. Different simplest ratios mean the shapes are not similar.

questions.question: Subtracting the same number of millimetres from both the width and the height of a rectangle always produces a similar rectangle.
questions.explanation: Image B shows the opposite: 20 mm was subtracted from both sides of A, yet the factors became 2/3 and 1/2, so B looks distorted. Only multiplying both sides by the same factor keeps similarity.

questions.question: Select ALL the changes to a 60 mm × 40 mm image that keep it similar to the original.
options: Multiply both width and height by ½
Multiply both width and height by 3/2
Subtract 20 mm from both width and height
Add 20 mm to both width and height
questions.explanation: Similarity needs the SAME multiplying factor on both sides (×½ gives C, ×3/2 gives D). Adding or subtracting the same amount, or scaling one side only, changes the ratio.

questions.question: In the ratio 60 : 40, what are the numbers 60 and 40 called?
questions.explanation: The chapter defines the two numbers in a : b as the terms of the ratio.

questions.question: What does a ratio written as a : b tell us?
options: The first quantity exceeds the second quantity by exactly a − b units
The second quantity is always a times as large as the first quantity
The two quantities together add up to a + b units in every situation
For every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second
questions.explanation: Example: image A is 60 : 40, so for every 60 mm of width there are 40 mm of height. A ratio compares by multiplication, not by difference.

questions.question: To reduce a ratio to its simplest form, we divide both terms by their…
questions.explanation: Dividing both terms by their highest common factor (HCF) gives the smallest whole-number terms, e.g. 60 : 40 ÷ 20 → 3 : 2.

questions.question: What is the simplest form of the ratio 90 : 60 (image D)?
questions.explanation: The HCF of 90 and 60 is 30; 90 ÷ 30 = 3 and 60 ÷ 30 = 2. (9 : 6 still shares the factor 3; 2 : 3 reverses the order.)

questions.question: In the chapter's school there are 5 teachers and 170 students. What is the teacher-to-student ratio in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Divide both terms by 5: 170 ÷ 5 = 34, so 5 : 170 = 1 : 34.

questions.question: Anagh mixes 600 mL of orange juice with 900 mL of apple juice. What is the ratio of orange juice to apple juice in simplest form?
questions.explanation: HCF of 600 and 900 is 300: 600 ÷ 300 = 2, 900 ÷ 300 = 3. Keep the order orange : apple. (2 : 5 is the fraction of the whole drink, not the ratio.)

questions.question: In Anagh's drink (600 mL orange, 900 mL apple), what FRACTION of the whole drink is orange juice?
questions.explanation: The whole is 600 + 900 = 1500 mL; 600/1500 = 2/5. The ratio 2 : 3 compares orange to apple, not orange to the whole — 2/3 is the common slip.

questions.question: Which of these ratios is NOT written in its simplest form?
questions.explanation: 21 and 6 share the factor 3, so 21 : 6 = 7 : 2. In 7 : 12, 3 : 4 and 5 : 4 the terms have HCF 1.

questions.question: The ratio 40 : 60 describes the same relationship as 60 : 40 because both use the same two numbers.
questions.explanation: Order matters: 60 : 40 means 60 of the first for every 40 of the second (3 : 2), while 40 : 60 is 2 : 3. The exercise item 7 : 12 :: 12 : 7 is false for the same reason.

questions.question: Dividing both terms of a ratio by the same number gives a ratio that is proportional to the original ratio.
questions.explanation: 60 : 40 ÷ 20 gives 3 : 2 and 90 : 60 ÷ 30 also gives 3 : 2 — dividing by a common factor keeps the ratios proportional.

questions.question: Which symbol does the chapter use to show that two ratios are proportional, as in 60 : 40 __ 30 : 20?
questions.explanation: a : b :: c : d indicates that the ratios a : b and c : d are proportional, e.g. 60 : 40 :: 30 : 20.

questions.question: When two ratios are the same in their simplest forms, we say that the ratios are…
questions.explanation: Two ratios with the same simplest form are called proportional, or in proportion.

questions.question: Are the ratios 3 : 4 and 72 : 96 proportional?
questions.explanation: Divide 72 and 96 by their HCF 24 to get 3 : 4, the same as the first ratio. Proportionality is about equal factors, not equal differences.

questions.question: Nitin built a 60 ft wall with 3 bags of cement; Hari built a 40 ft wall with 2 bags. What should Nitin conclude?
options: Hari's wall is weaker because 2 bags is less than 3 bags
Nitin's wall is weaker because 60 : 3 is larger than 40 : 2
Hari's wall is stronger because 40 : 2 reduces to 10 : 1
Both ratios reduce to 20 : 1, so the walls are equally strong
questions.explanation: 60 : 3 = 20 : 1 and 40 : 2 = 20 : 1 — each used the same cement per foot of wall, so Nitin should not worry.

questions.question: Why is the statement 8 : 3 :: 24 : 6 FALSE?
options: 24 is 3 × 8 but 6 is only 2 × 3 — the terms changed by different factors
The cross products 8 × 6 and 3 × 24 are both equal to 48
24 − 8 = 16 but 6 − 3 = 3 — the differences are not equal
24 : 6 reduces to 8 : 3 but 8 : 3 cannot be reduced further
questions.explanation: For a true proportion both terms must change by the same factor. 8 → 24 is ×3 while 3 → 6 is ×2 (cross products 48 ≠ 72). Differences are irrelevant.

questions.question: Is 24 : 8 :: 9 : 3 a true proportion?
options: No, 24 is not a multiple of 9
questions.explanation: 24 ÷ 8 = 3 and 9 ÷ 3 = 3, so both are 3 : 1 (cross products 24 × 3 = 72 = 8 × 9). The factor between the ratios is 3/8 — it need not be a whole number.

questions.question: In a brick-wall pattern, one repeating block has 2 + 3 + 4 grey bricks and 3 + 2 + 1 coloured bricks. What is the ratio of grey to coloured bricks in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Grey = 9, coloured = 6, so 9 : 6; dividing by the HCF 3 gives 3 : 2. Because the pattern repeats, the whole wall has the same ratio.

questions.question: In the second brick-wall pattern, one block has 16 grey bricks and 12 coloured bricks. What is the ratio of grey to coloured bricks in simplest form?
questions.explanation: 16 : 12, divided by the HCF 4, is 4 : 3. (8 : 6 is not fully reduced; 3 : 4 reverses the order.)

questions.question: Select ALL the statements of proportion that are TRUE.
questions.explanation: 4 : 7 → ×3 gives 12 : 21 (4 × 21 = 7 × 12 = 84). 21 : 6 and 35 : 10 both reduce to 7 : 2 (21 × 10 = 6 × 35 = 210). The others fail the cross-product test.

questions.question: 7 : 12 :: 12 : 7 is a true proportion because both ratios use the same two numbers.
questions.explanation: Order matters. 7 : 12 and 12 : 7 are different relationships, and cross-multiplying gives 7 × 7 = 49 ≠ 12 × 12 = 144.

questions.question: Kesang used 10 spoons of sugar for 6 glasses of lemonade. How many spoons keep the same sweetness for 18 glasses?
questions.explanation: 6 : 10 :: 18 : ?. The first term grew by the factor 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so the sugar must also triple: 10 × 3 = 30. Adding 12 (6 → 18) to get 22 is the additive slip.

questions.question: Which ratio with second term 42 is proportional to 14 : 21?
questions.explanation: 42 is 2 × 21, so the first term must be 2 × 14 = 28. (21 : 42 = 1 : 2 and 35 : 42 = 5 : 6 are different from 2 : 3.)

questions.question: Fill the blank so that 6 : ___ is proportional to 14 : 21.
questions.explanation: 14y = 6 gives y = 6/14 = 3/7, and 21 × 3/7 = 9. Subtracting 8 from both terms (14 → 6, 21 → 13) is the trap — ratios change by multiplication.

questions.question: Fill the blank so that 2 : ___ is proportional to 14 : 21.
questions.explanation: 14 ÷ 7 = 2, so divide 21 by the same 7 to get 3. In fact 2 : 3 is the simplest form of 14 : 21.

questions.question: The ratios 3 : 4, 12 : ___, 20 : ___ and 27 : ___ are proportional to 18 : 24. What is the missing term in 12 : ___?
questions.explanation: 18 : 24 = 3 : 4, so the second term is 4/3 of the first: 12 × 4/3 = 16. (18 would come from adding 6, the slip.)

questions.question: Which value makes 20 : ___ proportional to 18 : 24?
questions.explanation: The second term is 4/3 of the first: 20 × 4/3 = 80/3 = 26⅔. Proportional terms need not be whole numbers; 81/3 = 27 and 84/3 = 28 are near-misses.

questions.question: Select ALL the ratios that are proportional to 4 : 9.
questions.explanation: Multiply both terms by the same factor: ×2 → 8 : 18, ×3 → 12 : 27 (the book also gives ×4 → 16 : 36). 8 : 13 adds 4 to both; 9 : 4 reverses the order; 16 : 32 is 1 : 2.

questions.question: When Neelima was 3, her mother was 10 times her age. What was the ratio of Neelima's age to her mother's age in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Mother's age = 3 × 10 = 30, so the ratio is 3 : 30 = 1 : 10.

questions.question: Nine years later Neelima is 12 and her mother is 39. What is the ratio of their ages now in simplest form?
questions.explanation: 12 : 39 ÷ 3 = 4 : 13. It is no longer 1 : 10 because 9 years were ADDED to both ages, not multiplied.

questions.question: Why did the Neelima–mother age ratio change from 1 : 10 to 4 : 13?
options: The mother's age was not exactly 10 times 12 because of a rounding slip
The starting ratio 1 : 10 was never in its simplest form to begin with
Ages must always be compared in months rather than in years
9 was added to both terms, not multiplied — so the ratio is not preserved
questions.explanation: Adding (or subtracting) the same number to both terms changes a ratio; only multiplying both terms by the same factor keeps it proportional.

questions.question: Harmain is 1 year old and her brother is 5. How old will Harmain be when the ratio of her age to her brother's is 1 : 2?
questions.explanation: After x years (1 + x) : (5 + x) = 1 : 2 → 2(1 + x) = 5 + x → x = 3. Harmain will be 1 + 3 = 4 (and her brother 8). '3 years' is the time, not her age.

questions.question: In how many years from now will Harmain (1) be exactly half her brother's (5) age?
questions.explanation: 2(1 + x) = 5 + x gives x = 3: in 3 years the ages are 4 and 8. The common slip is answering 4, which is Harmain's age at that time.

questions.question: At which later pair of ages will Neelima and her mother again be in the ratio 1 : 10?
questions.explanation: Both gain the same number of years, so the 27-year gap stays fixed while the ratio keeps changing — 1 : 10 (gap 27 at 3 and 30) never returns. 6 and 60 would need a 54-year gap.

questions.question: Adding the same number to both terms of a ratio always gives a ratio proportional to the original.
questions.explanation: 3 : 30 = 1 : 10, but adding 9 gives 12 : 39 = 4 : 13 — a different ratio. The chapter states the ratio 'is not necessarily proportional' after adding.

questions.question: Multiplying both terms of a ratio by the same fraction, such as 3/7, gives a ratio proportional to the original.
questions.explanation: 14 : 21 × 3/7 gives 6 : 9, which the chapter shows is proportional to 14 : 21. The factor need not be a whole number.

questions.question: Select ALL the operations that keep a ratio proportional to 14 : 21.
options: Multiplying only the second term by 2
questions.explanation: ×2 gives 28 : 42 and ÷7 gives 2 : 3, both proportional. Adding/subtracting 7 (21 : 28, 7 : 14) or scaling one term only changes the ratio.

questions.question: Manjunath's regular filter coffee uses 15 mL decoction with 35 mL milk. What is the decoction-to-milk ratio in simplest form?
For 'stronger' coffee he mixes 20 mL decoction with 30 mL milk. What is this ratio in simplest form?
questions.explanation: 20 : 30 ÷ 10 = 2 : 3. (1 : 4 is the light coffee 10 : 40.)

questions.question: Why is the 20 : 30 coffee stronger than the regular 15 : 35 coffee?
options: 20 : 30 has a bigger HCF than 15 : 35, so the coffee is stronger
There is more decoction for every mL of milk (2/3 instead of 3/7)
20 + 30 = 50 is the same total volume as 15 + 35, so it tastes stronger
Milk alone decides strength, and 30 mL is less than 35 mL
questions.explanation: Strength depends on the proportion of decoction to milk: 2/3 ≈ 0.67 mL of decoction per mL of milk versus 3/7 ≈ 0.43 for regular coffee.

questions.question: In the table, 300 mL decoction is mixed with 600 mL milk. Compared with regular coffee (15 : 35), this coffee is…
options: Regular — 300 and 600 are both 20 times the regular amounts
Stronger — 1 : 2 has more decoction per mL of milk than 3 : 7
Lighter — 1 : 2 has less decoction per mL of milk than 3 : 7
questions.explanation: 300 : 600 = 1 : 2 = 0.5 decoction per mL of milk; regular is 3/7 ≈ 0.43. More decoction per mL of milk means stronger. (20 × 35 = 700, not 600.)

questions.question: 150 mL decoction with 500 mL milk gives which kind of coffee compared with regular 15 : 35?
questions.explanation: 150 : 500 = 3 : 10 = 0.3 decoction per mL of milk, less than regular's 3/7 ≈ 0.43, so it is lighter.

questions.question: 24 mL decoction with 56 mL milk is…
questions.explanation: 24 : 56 ÷ 8 = 3 : 7, exactly the regular recipe 15 : 35.

questions.question: Which statement about 100 mL decoction with 300 mL milk is correct?
options: Exactly the same strength as the light recipe 10 : 40
Lighter than regular 3 : 7 but stronger than light 1 : 4
Lighter than both the regular coffee and the light recipe
Stronger than both the regular coffee and the light recipe
questions.explanation: 100 : 300 = 1 : 3 ≈ 0.33 decoction per mL of milk. That is below regular (3/7 ≈ 0.43) but above the light recipe (1/4 = 0.25).

questions.question: Select ALL the mixes (decoction : milk, in mL) that are STRONGER than regular coffee 15 : 35.
questions.explanation: 300 : 600 and 200 : 400 are both 1 : 2 (0.5 decoction per mL of milk) > 3/7. 150 : 500 (0.3) and 100 : 300 (0.33) are lighter; 24 : 56 equals 3 : 7 (regular).

questions.question: Light coffee made with 10 mL decoction and 40 mL milk has a decoction-to-milk ratio of 1 : 4 in simplest form.
questions.explanation: 10 : 40 ÷ 10 = 1 : 4, which has less decoction per mL of milk than regular 3 : 7, so it is lighter.

questions.question: Coffee made with 200 mL decoction and 400 mL milk is lighter than regular coffee because it uses far more milk (400 mL instead of 35 mL).
questions.explanation: Strength depends on the RATIO, not the absolute amount of milk. 200 : 400 = 1 : 2 has more decoction per mL of milk than 3 : 7, so it is stronger.

questions.question: If a : b :: c : d, which equation always holds?
questions.explanation: Because c = fa and d = fb for the same factor f, c/a = d/b; multiplying both sides by ab gives bc = ad. This is cross multiplication.

questions.question: In a : b :: c : d, the unknown fourth term d equals…
questions.explanation: From ad = bc, divide both sides by a: d = bc/a — multiply the two middle terms and divide by the first.

questions.question: In a 'Rule of Three' problem, how many of the four proportional quantities are known?
questions.explanation: Four quantities are linked proportionally; three are given and the fourth must be found — hence the name Rule of Three (Trairāśika).

questions.question: In Āryabhaṭa's Rule of Three, the given 'measure' (our term a) is called the…
questions.explanation: pramāṇa = measure (a), phala = fruit (b), ichchhā = requisition (c), ichchhāphala = yield (d).

questions.question: Which sentence states Āryabhaṭa's rule for finding the yield (ichchhāphala)?
options: Multiply the phala by the pramāṇa and divide by the ichchhā
Add the phala to the ichchhā and divide by the pramāṇa
Multiply the phala by the ichchhā and divide by the pramāṇa
Multiply the pramāṇa by the ichchhā and divide by the phala
questions.explanation: ichchhāphala = (phala × ichchhā) ÷ pramāṇa, which is exactly d = bc/a in modern notation.

questions.question: For the mid-day meal, 15 kg of rice feeds 120 students. On a rainy day only 80 students come. How much rice should the cook make?
A car covers 90 km in 150 minutes. At the same speed, how far does it travel in 4 hours?
questions.explanation: Convert 4 h to 240 min, then 150 : 90 :: 240 : x → x = 240 × 90 ÷ 150 = 144 km. (Using 4 instead of 240 would give a meaningless answer.)

questions.question: WHY does ad = bc hold whenever a : b :: c : d?
options: Because a × b always equals c × d when ratios are proportional
Because d is always the largest of the four terms in a proportion
c = f × a and d = f × b for the same factor f, so c/a = d/b
Because a + d always equals b + c when ratios are proportional
questions.explanation: Both terms change by the same factor f, giving f = c/a = d/b; multiplying both sides by ab yields bc = ad.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct matches between Āryabhaṭa's terms and a : b :: c : d.
questions.explanation: pramāṇa = a (measure), phala = b (fruit), ichchhā = c (requisition), ichchhāphala = d (yield).

questions.question: In a : b :: c : d, the term c must always be a whole-number multiple of a.
questions.explanation: The factor can be a fraction: in 120 : 15 :: 80 : 10 the factor is 2/3, and in 14 : 21 :: 6 : 9 it is 3/7.

questions.question: Why is 150 : 90 :: 4 : ? the WRONG way to set up the car problem (90 km in 150 minutes, distance in 4 hours)?
options: 90 km should first be converted into metres before forming the ratio
Distance should be written first in both ratios, not time
4 hours is far too small a number to compare with 150 minutes
150 is in minutes but 4 is in hours — both ratios must use the same unit
questions.explanation: Time appears in both ratios, so it must be in the same unit: 4 hours = 240 minutes, giving 150 : 90 :: 240 : ?.

questions.question: How many minutes are there in 4 hours?
questions.explanation: 4 × 60 = 240 minutes — the conversion needed before applying the Rule of Three in Example 9.

questions.question: Himachal tea: 200 g for ₹200. Meghalaya tea: 1 kg for ₹800. In grams, what are the two weight-to-price ratios in simplest form?
questions.explanation: 200 : 200 = 1 : 1. Convert 1 kg to 1000 g: 1000 : 800 = 5 : 4. The ratios are not proportional.

questions.question: Which tea is more expensive, and why?
options: Neither — the ratios 1 : 1 and 5 : 4 are proportional, so prices match
Meghalaya — a 1 kg packet always costs more than a 200 g packet
Himachal — 1 kg would cost ₹1,000, more than Meghalaya's ₹800
Meghalaya — ₹800 for a packet is more than ₹200 for a packet
questions.explanation: Compare the price for the SAME weight: 200 g is 1/5 kg, so 1 kg of Himachal tea costs 200 × 5 = ₹1,000 > ₹800.

questions.question: The Earth travels about 940 million km around the Sun in a year. Roughly how far does it travel in one week?
questions.explanation: A year has 52 weeks: 940,000,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 18,076,923 km. Dividing by 365 (≈2.6 million) or 12 (≈78 million) uses the wrong unit.

questions.question: A mason needs about 1450 bricks for a 10 ft wall. The outer and inner walls of a house total 108 ft. How many bricks are needed?
Delhi: 1,484 sq km, about 30 million people. Mumbai: 550 sq km, about 20 million. Which city is more crowded?
options: Delhi — its area of 1,484 sq km is much larger than Mumbai's
Mumbai — about 20,000 people per sq km versus about 36,000 in Delhi
Mumbai — about 36,000 people per sq km versus about 20,000 in Delhi
Delhi — 30 million people is more than 20 million people
questions.explanation: Compare people per sq km: Delhi 30,000,000 ÷ 1484 ≈ 20,216; Mumbai 20,000,000 ÷ 550 ≈ 36,364. Mumbai packs more people into each sq km.

questions.question: To decide which tea is more expensive, the chapter compares the prices for the same weight of tea.
questions.explanation: Prices are only comparable for equal weights; that is why the cost of 1 kg of Himachal tea (₹1,000) is worked out and compared with ₹800.

questions.question: The weight-to-price ratio of Meghalaya tea can be written as 1 : 800 and compared directly with Himachal's 200 : 200.
questions.explanation: 1 : 800 mixes kilograms with the grams used for Himachal. Convert to grams first: 1000 : 800 = 5 : 4.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: Puneeth's father rode from Lucknow to Kanpur in 2 hours at 50 km/h. Why can't 50 : 2 :: 75 : ? give the time at 75 km/h?
options: 75 km/h is not a whole-number multiple of 50 km/h
Speed and time are measured in two different units
The distance between Lucknow and Kanpur is not given
Time DECREASES as speed increases — not a direct proportion
questions.explanation: The Rule of Three assumes both quantities grow by the same factor. Here a faster speed means LESS time, so the proportion model fails.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: Using the chapter's data (2 hours at 50 km/h), how far is Kanpur from Lucknow?
questions.explanation: Distance = speed × time = 50 × 2 = 100 km.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: How long would Puneeth's father take at 75 km/h for the 100 km trip?
questions.explanation: 100 ÷ 75 = 4/3 hours = 80 minutes. The wrong Rule of Three (50 : 2 :: 75 : 3) gives 3 hours — more time for a faster ride, which is absurd.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: Shampoo sachet: 6 mL for ₹2. Small bottle: 180 mL for ₹154. Is price proportional to volume?
questions.explanation: Volume grows 30 times but price grows 77 times, so the ratios are not proportional.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: Sachet 6 mL ₹2; small 180 mL ₹154; medium 340 mL ₹276; large 1000 mL ₹540. Which container is CHEAPEST per mL?
questions.explanation: Price per mL: sachet 2/6 ≈ ₹0.33, small ≈ ₹0.86, medium ≈ ₹0.81, large ₹0.54. Surprisingly the sachet is cheapest per mL in this sample table.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: From the same shampoo table, which container is the MOST expensive per mL?
questions.explanation: 154 ÷ 180 ≈ ₹0.86 per mL, higher than medium (≈ ₹0.81), large (₹0.54) and sachet (≈ ₹0.33).

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: A tractor ploughs 4 times faster than a pair of oxen, which take 6 hours per acre. How long does the tractor take per acre?
questions.explanation: Faster means LESS time: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 hours. Multiplying (6 × 4 = 24) is the Rule-of-Three trap for an inverse situation.

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: The farmer's field is 20 acres. How long would the pair of oxen and the tractor each take?
questions.explanation: Oxen: 20 × 6 = 120 h. Tractor: 20 × 1.5 = 30 h (one quarter of the oxen's time).

questions.topic: When Rule of Three Does Not Apply
questions.question: Every problem that gives three related numbers and asks for a fourth can be solved with the Rule of Three.
questions.explanation: The speed–time problem (50 km/h, 2 h, 75 km/h) looks like a Rule of Three but is not: time falls as speed rises, so 50 : 2 :: 75 : ? is invalid.

questions.question: Two friends share 12 counters equally. What is the ratio of their counters in simplest form?
questions.explanation: Each gets 6, so the ratio is 6 : 6 = 1 : 1.

questions.question: If your partner takes 5 of the 12 counters, what is the ratio of your partner's counters to yours?
questions.explanation: You get 12 − 5 = 7, so partner : you = 5 : 7 (already in simplest form).

questions.question: 12 counters are shared in the ratio 3 : 1. How many does each person get?
questions.explanation: Hand out 3 and 1 repeatedly: three rounds use all 12, giving 9 and 3. Equivalently 12 ÷ 4 = 3 per group, so 3 × 3 = 9 and 1 × 3 = 3.

questions.question: A quantity x is divided in the ratio m : n. What is the first part?
questions.explanation: x is split into m + n equal groups of size x/(m + n); the first share has m of these groups. x/(m + n) alone is just one group.

questions.question: Prashanti invested ₹75,000 and Bhuvan ₹25,000. A profit of ₹4,000 is shared in the ratio of their investments. What is Prashanti's share?
Divide ₹4,500 into two parts in the ratio 2 : 3.
Acid and water are mixed in the ratio 1 : 5. How much of each is in 240 mL of the solution?
questions.explanation: 6 groups of 240 ÷ 6 = 40 mL: acid 1 × 40 = 40 mL, water 5 × 40 = 200 mL. Treating 240 as the water (not the whole) is the slip.

questions.question: Soft idlis need rice and urad dal in the ratio 2 : 1. For 6 cups of mixture, how much of each is needed?
questions.explanation: 3 groups of 6 ÷ 3 = 2 cups: rice 2 × 2 = 4 cups, dal 1 × 2 = 2 cups.

questions.question: A crane 155 cm tall has its neck and the rest of its body in the ratio 4 : 6. How long is its neck?
questions.explanation: Neck = 4/(4 + 6) × 155 = 4/10 × 155 = 62 cm; the rest is 93 cm. Picking 93 confuses neck with body.

questions.question: A ₹10 coin has mass 7.74 g and is copper and nickel in the ratio 3 : 1. What is the mass of copper in it?
Copper costs ₹906 per kg and nickel ₹1,341 per kg. What is the approximate total value of the metal in the 7.74 g ₹10 coin?
questions.explanation: Copper: 5.805 g × 906/1000 ≈ ₹5.26; nickel: 1.935 g × 1341/1000 ≈ ₹2.59; total ≈ ₹7.85 — less than the coin's face value.

questions.question: Dividing 12 counters in the ratio 3 : 1 means one person gets 3 counters and the other gets 1.
questions.explanation: 3 : 1 is the ratio of the shares, not the shares themselves: 12 ÷ (3 + 1) = 3 per group, so the shares are 9 and 3.

questions.question: 42 counters are shared in the ratio 4 : 3. Select ALL the correct statements.
questions.explanation: 4 + 3 = 7 groups of 42 ÷ 7 = 6 counters each; shares are 24 and 18. 28 and 21 come from wrong group sizes.

questions.question: A 40 kg mixture has sand and cement in the ratio 3 : 1. How much sand does it contain?
How much cement must be ADDED to the original 40 kg mixture (3 : 1) to make the ratio 5 : 2?
questions.explanation: New cement needed is 12 kg and 10 kg is already present, so add 12 − 10 = 2 kg. (12 kg is the total, not the addition.)

questions.question: In Example 12, why does the sand remain 30 kg in the new mixture?
options: Only cement is added — the quantity of sand is not changed
Sand is always 3/4 of any sand-and-cement mixture
The new ratio 5 : 2 also gives 30 kg of sand for a 40 kg mixture
Both sand and cement are added in the ratio 5 : 2
questions.explanation: The question adds cement only, so sand stays at 30 kg and the cement must rise to 2/5 × 30 = 12 kg. (5/7 of 40 is about 28.6, not 30.)

questions.question: Blue and yellow paints are mixed in the ratio 3 : 5. How much of each is needed for 40 mL of green paint?
questions.explanation: 8 groups of 40 ÷ 8 = 5 mL: blue 3 × 5 = 15 mL, yellow 5 × 5 = 25 mL.

questions.question: To the 40 mL of green paint (15 mL blue, 25 mL yellow) 20 mL of yellow is added. What is the new blue-to-yellow ratio?
questions.explanation: Blue stays 15 mL; yellow becomes 25 + 20 = 45 mL. 15 : 45 = 1 : 3 — lighter green than 3 : 5.

questions.question: A bucket of orange paint is red and yellow in the ratio 3 : 5. A second, equal-sized bucket full of yellow paint is poured in. What is the new red-to-yellow ratio?
questions.explanation: Red is 3/8 of a bucket and yellow 5/8; adding a whole bucket of yellow gives 5/8 + 1 = 13/8. So red : yellow = 3/8 : 13/8 = 3 : 13.

questions.question: Adding more of only one ingredient to a mixture leaves the ratio of the ingredients unchanged.
questions.explanation: Adding 20 mL of yellow changed blue : yellow from 3 : 5 to 1 : 3; adding 2 kg of cement changed 3 : 1 to 5 : 2. Only adding BOTH in the same ratio keeps it unchanged.

questions.question: After adding 2 kg of cement in Example 12, the mixture weighs 42 kg with 30 kg sand and 12 kg cement, which is in the ratio 5 : 2.
Select ALL the actions that CHANGE the ratio of a 3 : 5 blue-to-yellow paint mix.
options: Adding 20 mL of yellow paint only
Doubling both the blue and the yellow
Adding 10 mL of blue paint only
Halving both the blue and the yellow
Making 80 mL with 30 mL blue and 50 mL yellow
questions.explanation: Adding one colour alone changes the ratio. Doubling or halving both, or using 30 : 50 (= 3 : 5), keeps the ratio the same.

questions.question: According to the chapter's conversion table, 1 metre equals how many feet?
questions.explanation: 1 metre = 3.281 feet. 2.471 is acres per hectare and 10.764 is square feet per square metre.

questions.question: 1 hectare equals how many square metres?
questions.explanation: 1 hectare = 10,000 square metres (and 2.471 acres). 43,560 is the number of square feet in an acre.

questions.question: 1 acre equals how many square feet?
questions.explanation: 1 acre = 43,560 square feet — the figure used in the manure and land-price exercises.

questions.question: 1 litre equals…
questions.explanation: 1 mL = 1 cubic centimetre, so 1 litre = 1,000 mL = 1,000 cc.

questions.question: Using Fahrenheit = 9/5 × Celsius + 32, what is 25 °C in Fahrenheit?
questions.explanation: 9/5 × 25 = 45; 45 + 32 = 77 °F. Forgetting the +32 gives 45; adding 32 without scaling gives 57.

questions.question: Using Celsius = 5/9 × (Fahrenheit − 32), what is 50 °F in Celsius?
questions.explanation: 50 − 32 = 18; 5/9 × 18 = 10 °C. Stopping at 18 or scaling 50 directly (≈ 28) are the common slips.

questions.question: Why is the Celsius–Fahrenheit conversion NOT a simple proportion like metres to feet?
options: 0 °C is 32 °F, not 0 °F — the added 32 means doubling °C does not double °F
Fahrenheit degrees are larger than Celsius degrees, so no ratio exists
The factor 9/5 is a fraction, and proportions need whole-number factors
A temperature cannot be measured in two different systems at the same time
questions.explanation: In a proportion 0 maps to 0 and the terms change by one factor. Temperature has a shift of 32, so e.g. 25 °C → 77 °F but 50 °C → 122 °F (not 154 °F).

questions.question: Since 1 mL equals 1 cubic centimetre, a 500 mL mug holds 500 cc of water.
questions.explanation: The chapter's table gives 1 millilitre (mL) = 1 cubic centimetre (cc), so 500 mL = 500 cc.

questions.question: Doubling a temperature in degrees Celsius always doubles the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.explanation: 25 °C = 77 °F but 50 °C = 9/5 × 50 + 32 = 122 °F, not 154 °F. The +32 shift breaks the proportion.

questions.question: Select ALL the conversions that match the chapter's table.
questions.explanation: The table gives 1 sq m = 10.764 sq ft and 1 hectare = 2.471 acres. A hectare (not an acre) is 10,000 sq m; 1 m = 3.281 ft; 1 litre = 1,000 cc.

questions.question: Līlāvatī: 2½ palas of saffron cost 3/7 niskas. How much saffron can be bought for 9 niskas?
questions.explanation: 3/7 : 2½ :: 9 : x → x = 2.5 × 9 ÷ (3/7) = 2.5 × 21 = 52.5 palas. 21 is only the factor by which the money grew.

questions.question: This year 204 people are going, with 54 per bus. How many buses are needed, and will they all be full?
questions.explanation: 204 ÷ 54 ≈ 3.78, so 3 buses are not enough — 4 are needed. 4 × 54 = 216 seats, leaving 216 − 204 = 12 empty.

questions.question: Equal volumes of gold and water have masses in the ratio 37 : 2. If 1 litre of water has mass 1 kg, what is the mass of 1 litre of gold?
questions.explanation: 37 : 2 :: x : 1 → x = 37 × 1 ÷ 2 = 18.5 kg. Reading 37 directly ignores the '2' in the water term.

questions.question: A tap fills a 500 mL mug in 15 seconds. How long does it take to fill a 10-litre bucket?
questions.explanation: 10 L = 10,000 mL = 20 mugs, so 20 × 15 = 300 seconds = 5 minutes. Treating 10 L as 10 mugs gives 2.5 minutes.

questions.question: Good practice is 10 tonnes of cow manure per acre. A plot is 200 ft by 500 ft. About how much manure is needed? (1 acre = 43,560 sq ft)
questions.explanation: Area = 100,000 sq ft = 100,000 ÷ 43,560 ≈ 2.3 acres, so manure ≈ 2.3 × 10 ≈ 23 tonnes (the key gives 22,956.8 kg).

questions.question: One acre of land costs ₹15,00,000. What is the cost of 2,400 square feet of the same land?
In the bus problem, 204 ÷ 54 is not a whole number, so the fourth bus will not be completely full.
questions.explanation: 3 buses hold only 162; 4 buses hold 216, so 12 seats remain vacant.

questions.question: The Earth travels about 940 million km in a year, so in a week it travels about 940 ÷ 12 ≈ 78 million km.
questions.explanation: A year has 52 weeks, not 12. 940 million ÷ 52 ≈ 18.1 million km per week; dividing by 12 gives the distance per MONTH.

questions.question: Select ALL the results that correctly follow from the chapter's exercises.
options: 1 litre of gold has a mass of 18.5 kg
A 200 ft × 500 ft plot is about 2.3 acres
2,400 sq ft of land costs about ₹1,50,000
questions.explanation: Gold: 37/2 = 18.5 kg. Plot: 100,000 ÷ 43,560 ≈ 2.3 acres. The bucket takes 5 minutes, the land costs about ₹82,645 and 4 buses leave 12 seats empty.

questions.question: Which statement from the chapter summary is NOT correct?
options: In a : b, for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second
Two ratios are proportional if their terms differ by the same amount
If x is divided in the ratio m : n, the first part is m × x/(m + n)
a : b :: c : d means that ad = bc
questions.explanation: Proportional ratios have terms that change by the same FACTOR (ad = bc), not by the same difference — the Neelima example shows adding breaks the ratio.

questions.question: If a : b :: c : d, select ALL the relations that must be true.
questions.explanation: Both terms change by the same factor f, so c/a = d/b = f, and cross-multiplying gives ad = bc. Sums, differences and the products ab, cd are not fixed.

questions.question: The summary states that a : b and c : d are proportional, written a : b :: c : d, if ad = bc.
questions.explanation: This is the cross-multiplication condition derived in Section 7.4 and repeated in the summary.

questions.question: The logic puzzle Binairo described at the end of the chapter is also known as…
questions.explanation: The chapter says 'Binairo, also known as Takuzu, is a logic puzzle with simple rules.'

questions.question: In Binairo, what must be true of every row and every column?
options: It has more horizontal lines than vertical lines
It has at least one horizontal and one vertical line
It has only horizontal lines or only vertical lines
It has an equal number of horizontal and vertical lines
questions.explanation: Rule 1: each row and each column must contain an equal number of horizontal and vertical lines.

questions.question: In Binairo, at most how many identical lines (all horizontal or all vertical) may sit next to each other?
questions.explanation: Rule 2: more than two horizontal or vertical lines can't be adjacent, so at most two in a row.

questions.question: In a 6 × 6 Binairo grid, how many horizontal lines must each row contain?
questions.explanation: Each row needs equal numbers of the two symbols, so 6 ÷ 2 = 3 horizontal and 3 vertical lines.

questions.question: Writing H for horizontal and V for vertical, which 6-cell row obeys the Binairo rules?
questions.explanation: HHVVHV has 3 H and 3 V with no run longer than two. HHHVVV has three H adjacent; HVHVHH has 4 H; VVHHVV has 4 V.

questions.question: In Binairo, two rows may be identical as long as every column is different.
questions.explanation: Rule 3 requires each row to be unique AND each column to be unique.
